issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a single-patient assault trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because it implies multiple victims or identification with other victims rather than the patient's own assault experience. A more self-referential trigger would be expected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
issues.explanation: 'Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening' sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile's self-directed shame and identity-change appraisals. It implies confidence that another person would have prevented the assault, which conflicts with the patient's own vulnerability/self-blame framing in a way that is hard to integrate clinically.

issues.item: Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma in a 70-year-old male, 'medical procedures' plus 'body shame' implies a strong bodily injury/medical aftermath theme, but the rest of the profile does not support that theme. With only offender cues and intrusive thoughts otherwise present, the medical trigger looks insufficiently anchored and may be mismatched to the rest of the assault profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Body shame' is not impossible after assault, but alongside 'defective self' and 'unrecognisable self' it suggests a bodily violation/injury-focused appraisal pattern that is not well reflected in the other selected nodes. The triggers and strategies mainly reflect avoidance, numbing, and offender-related activation rather than body-focused trauma processing.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
issues.explanation: 'Catastrophising others' is weakly connected to the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation links Triggers strongly with Maladaptive Strategies and Negative Appraisals strongly with Triggers, but this strategy is not a plausible direct response to the chosen triggers (medical procedures, intrusive thoughts, offender cues) and is not well explained by the selected appraisals. It addresses a generalized harm concern that is otherwise absent from the profile.

vignette:
Harold was seventy years old, a salesman his whole working life, and he had never thought of himself as a man who startled easily. But now, three years after the assault, he could not walk past the liquor store on Cherry Street without his chest tightening. The smell of alcohol—bourbon, mostly—came at him from doorways, from the breath of a stranger on the bus, and each time the memory hit him not as a thought but as a physical drop: the weight of a hand on his shoulder, the cheap cologne, the voice that said something he could never quite recall. What he recalled instead was what came after—the concrete floor, the pain in his ribs, the taste of his own blood.

It had happened after a sales call that had gone badly. Harold had stopped at a bar near the office—a place he used to go for a beer after work, to decompress before heading home to his wife, Eleanor. That night he had one drink, then another, frustrated with himself for botching the pitch. A younger man at the next stool started talking, friendly at first, then pushy. Harold did not remember exactly what he said in response—he had tried to deflect, to laugh it off—but the man followed him into the parking lot. The assault lasted maybe two minutes. Harold did not fight back. He had frozen, his arms at his sides, and taken the blows until someone shouted from a window and the man ran.

In the months afterward, Harold found himself driving an extra six blocks to avoid that parking lot. He stopped going anywhere near the bar. Then he stopped going to any bar, even for a quick bite with colleagues, because the smell of alcohol from the grill made his throat close. He told Eleanor he was cutting back for his health. She did not push. But the avoidance spread: he began leaving the office ten minutes early to avoid passing the liquor store on the way to the train. He took a different route home, adding twenty minutes to his commute. When a client suggested meeting at a brewpub, Harold invented a conflict. He told himself it was just easier that way. He did not mention the real reason—the fear that he might see the man again, that the man might recognize him. Harold knew his face was one of many, but still, every bald head, every heavy build in a leather jacket, made him scan the crowd, catalogue exits, hold his breath.

The suppression took a different toll. He would catch himself beginning to think about the assault—the concrete grit against his cheek—and he would force his mind elsewhere. He read the newspaper more intently. He turned the television on as soon as he walked in the door. He stopped letting his mind wander during his afternoon coffee break. But the thoughts still came, unwanted, at night mostly, when he lay in bed staring at the ceiling. He learned to keep his body still, his face blank, so that Eleanor would not ask what was wrong.

Harold had come to believe something was fundamentally wrong with him. He replayed the parking lot moment again and again: If I had just stood my ground. If I had said something different. If I had not had that second drink. The way he acted that night—passive, even cowardly—had caused the whole thing. He was certain of that. And the person he had become since—wary, hollow, always checking the rearview mirror—was someone he did not recognize. When he looked in the bathroom mirror in the morning, he saw a stranger. He had started to feel defective, as if the assault had not just hurt his body but had revealed something that had always been broken in him.

The emotional distance had crept into his marriage. He stopped telling Eleanor about his day. He stopped reaching for her hand on the couch. He was not cold—he simply felt nothing, or rather he made sure he felt nothing, because feeling anything seemed to risk opening a door he could not close. Eleanor asked him once if he was okay. He said he was fine. The word came out flat, and she did not ask again.

What finally brought Harold to a clinic was a moment at work. A customer, a man in his forties, ordered a drink at a business lunch and raised his glass toward Harold with a smile. The smell of bourbon hit Harold from across the table. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink, his hands shaking. He stayed there for ten minutes. When he came back, the client was gone. Harold drove home in silence, and that evening he told Eleanor he needed to talk to someone. He did not know if help was possible. He was afraid that the person he had become was permanent, and that whatever made him defective could not be fixed. But he also hoped—very quietly, almost without admitting it to himself—that maybe he could find a way back to the man he used to be before the parking lot, before the smell of bourbon meant anything more than a drink.
